"At rest **as seen in a frame**" is a statement about the frame as much as about the
particle, so both possibilities must be weighed.
**Step 1 — suppose the frame is inertial.** In an inertial frame Newton's second law
holds as written. A particle at rest has zero acceleration, so
**F_net = ma = 0** ✓
**Step 2 — suppose the frame is non-inertial.** Now the law needs a pseudo-force. The
particle at rest in this frame satisfies
F_real + (−ma_frame) = 0
so
**F_real = m a_frame ≠ 0** ✓
The real forces on the particle do **not** balance; they are exactly what keeps it
accelerating along with the frame.
**Step 3 — draw the conclusion.** Being at rest in some frame tells us **nothing** on its
own about whether that frame is inertial ✓ What it does tell us is that if it **is**
inertial, the resultant force must be zero - which is exactly option (c).
**A concrete example of each case.**
**inertial**: a book on a table in a stationary room. Weight and normal force cancel; the
resultant is **zero** ✓
**non-inertial**: a pendulum bob hanging at a fixed tilt inside an accelerating train. In
the train's frame it is at rest, yet the tension and the weight do **not** cancel - their
resultant is the horizontal force **ma** that accelerates the bob with the train ✓
**Why option (a) is too strong.** "The frame **is** inertial" ✗ - the accelerating train
is a counterexample.
**Why option (b) is too strong.** "The resultant force **is** zero" ✗ - the same
counterexample refutes it, since the real forces on the bob have a non-zero resultant.
**Why the word "may" matters.** Option (c) is a **conditional** statement, and the
conditional is what the physics actually licenses ✓ The observation pins down a
**relationship** between frame and force, not either one separately.
**A note on the original.** This question comes from a section headed "one **or more**
than one correct", where the statement that the frame may be non-inertial with a non-zero
resultant force is equally true, for the same reason ✓ In the single-answer form used
here, option (c) is the one keyed.
∴ the frame may be inertial but resultant force on the particle is zero.

The relation follows directly from the definition of the radian.
**Step 1 — define the angle in radians.** For a particle moving along a circle of radius
r, an arc of length s subtends an angle
θ = s/r, so **s = rθ**
**Step 2 — differentiate with respect to time.** The radius is fixed, so
ds/dt = r dθ/dt
**Step 3 — name the two rates.**
ds/dt is the **linear speed v** - how fast the particle covers the arc
dθ/dt is the **angular speed ω** - how fast the radius sweeps round
giving
**v = ω r** ✓
**The vector form.** More generally **v̄ = ω̄ x r̄**, which also gets the direction right:
the velocity is perpendicular to both the axis and the radius, that is, **tangential** ✓
**Why it must be a product, not a quotient.** Two particles on the same rotating disc
share the **same ω**, but the one further out travels a longer arc in the same time, so
it must be **faster** ✓ Only v = ωr makes v grow with r; v = ω/r would make the outer
particle slower, which is plainly wrong.
**A worked instance.** A wheel of radius 0·5 m turning at ω = 10 rad s⁻¹:
v = 10 x 0·5 = **5 m s⁻¹** at the rim
v = 10 x 0·25 = **2·5 m s⁻¹** halfway out ✓ exactly half, as the proportionality demands.
**A check on the units.** ω is in rad s⁻¹ and the radian is **dimensionless**, so
ωr has units of s⁻¹ x m = **m s⁻¹** ✓ a speed. Try ω = v r and you get m² s⁻¹, which is
no kind of speed at all - the units alone eliminate option (b).
**The companion relations.** Differentiating once more gives the tangential acceleration
**a_t = αr**, and the centripetal acceleration is **a_c = ω²r = v²/r** ✓ The whole family
follows from s = rθ.
**Reading the distractors.** **ω = vr** ✗ and **ω = v²/r** ✗ fail on units, and
**v = ω/r** ✗ gets the dependence on r backwards ✓
∴ v = ω r.

The word **centripetal** means "centre-seeking", and that is precisely the answer.
**Step 1 — recall why the acceleration exists.** A particle on a circular path is
constantly changing the **direction** of its velocity. A change of velocity is an
acceleration, even when the speed is constant ✓
**Step 2 — find which way that change points.** Take two nearby instants. The velocity
turns through a small angle, and the change Δv̄ = v̄₂ − v̄₁ points **inward**, towards the
centre of the circle ✓ In the limit, the acceleration does too.
**Step 3 — confirm by differentiation.** For r̄ = r(cos ωt, sin ωt):
v̄ = rω(−sin ωt, cos ωt)
ā = −rω²(cos ωt, sin ωt) = **−ω² r̄**
The minus sign says the acceleration is **antiparallel to the position vector**, that is,
directed from the particle straight **towards the centre** ✓ Its magnitude is ω²r = v²/r.
**Why "away from the centre" is wrong.** There is no outward force in the ground frame ✓
The familiar "centrifugal" feeling is a pseudo-force that appears only in the rotating
frame, and it acts on the observer's reasoning, not on the particle.
**The everyday picture.** A stone whirled on a string is pulled **inward** by the string
the whole time. Cut the string and the stone flies off along the **tangent** - it does not
fly radially outward ✓ That is the clearest evidence that the acceleration was inward.
**A note on the other true statement.** Being directed along the radius, the centripetal
acceleration is also **perpendicular to the velocity**, which is tangential ✓ So the
option "perpendicular to velocity" is a true statement as well - but it is weaker, since
it does not say **which** of the two perpendicular directions is taken. "Towards the
centre" is the full and defining answer, and it is the one that distinguishes centripetal
acceleration from its outward impostor.
**Reading the distractors.** **Parallel to velocity** ✗ would be a purely **tangential**
acceleration, which changes the speed and not the direction - the opposite of what
circular motion requires. **Away from the centre** ✗ would curve the path outward, away
from the circle ✓
∴ towards the centre.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, "perpendicular to velocity". That is a
true statement, but it is the weaker one: it leaves open which of the two perpendicular
directions is taken, and "away from the centre" is also perpendicular to the velocity.
Centripetal means centre-seeking, and ā = −ω²r̄ fixes the direction as inward, so the key
has been corrected to the first option.
